name: TRT clinics (online telehealth)
summary: Online and in-person clinics that prescribe testosterone replacement; mainstream medical sources cover TRT itself but little on telehealth providers.
lead: TRT clinics are medical practices, many operating online, that assess men for low testosterone and prescribe testosterone replacement therapy (TRT). TRT supplements or replaces androgens and can be delivered by injection, gel, patch, pellet or other forms .

name: Hormone bloodwork panel (total/free T, SHBG, E2, LH)
summary: The standard blood tests used to check testosterone status; clinical guidance exists, but interpreting free testosterone is technically contested.
lead: A hormone bloodwork panel typically includes total testosterone, free or bioavailable testosterone, sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), estradiol (E2) and luteinizing hormone (LH). Wikipedia describes a blood test as the way low testosterone is identified, with LH checked to find the cause .

name: Heavy compound lifting for testosterone
summary: Squats and deadlifts to push testosterone up; acute rises are documented, lasting baseline changes are not established in these sources.
lead: Heavy compound lifting for testosterone refers to the practice of performing large multi-joint barbell exercises such as squats and deadlifts with the stated aim of raising testosterone levels, which proponents associate with a more masculine physique and appearance. The idea is common in fitness and looksmaxxing discussions of lifestyle ways to support testosterone.

name: Losing body fat to raise testosterone
summary: Cutting fat to lift testosterone via less aromatase; the mechanism is described, but the BMI link is called unclear.
lead: Losing body fat to raise testosterone is the belief that reducing fat mass increases circulating testosterone in men, and so supports a leaner, more masculine appearance. Proponents link it to the way adipose tissue handles sex hormones.

name: Eating testicles / Rocky Mountain oysters
summary: Fried bull testicles eaten as a virility food; popular as lore, with no human data on testosterone.
lead: Eating testicles, often as Rocky Mountain oysters, is the practice of consuming animal testicles in the belief that they support male hormones or virility. Rocky Mountain oysters are a dish of bulls' testicles, usually skinned and deep-fried .

name: Raw eggs / oysters / zinc-rich foods
summary: Oysters and eggs for testosterone via zinc; deficiency lowers T, but extra zinc is reported not to raise it further.
lead: Raw eggs, oysters and other zinc-rich foods are eaten by some people in the belief that they raise testosterone. The reasoning rests mainly on zinc, a mineral needed to produce testosterone.

name: Cruciferous vegetables for estrogen
summary: Broccoli-family vegetables for estrogen balance via I3C; shown in animals and cells, thin in humans.
lead: The cruciferous vegetables for estrogen claim holds that eating broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower and similar vegetables, or supplements derived from them, shifts estrogen metabolism in a favourable direction, which some men pursue to limit estrogenic effects.

name: Avoiding soy ("soy boy" meta)
summary: Skipping soy to protect testosterone; meta-analyses report no hormonal effect in healthy men.
lead: Avoiding soy is the practice of limiting soy foods out of concern that their phytoestrogens lower testosterone or feminize men. The idea is tied to the online insult "soy boy", used for men seen as lacking masculine traits .

name: Avoiding plastics / BPA / phthalates
summary: Cutting down on plastic-linked 'xenoestrogens' (BPA, phthalates) to protect testosterone and body composition; the chemicals are real, the appearance payoff is unproven.
lead: Avoiding plastics, BPA and phthalates is a lifestyle practice in which people try to limit exposure to endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs), often called 'xenoestrogens' in looksmaxxing and fitness communities. Practitioners typically swap plastic food containers for glass or steel, avoid canned food and handling of thermal receipts, and choose fragrance-free or phthalate-free products.
claims: Xenoestrogens from plastics lower men's testosterone and cause gynecomastia and 'soy boy' features.
Switching to glass, steel and 'BPA-free' products removes the problem.
Handling receipts is a meaningful source of exposure.
Eating raw saturated fats, sweating or supporting the liver 'detoxes' xenoestrogens.

name: Testicular sun / red light exposure
summary: Shining sunlight or red light on the testes in hopes of higher testosterone; a fringe idea with no human trials behind it.
lead: Testicular sun or red light exposure is a fringe wellness practice in which men expose the scrotum to direct sunlight or to red or near-infrared lamps, in the belief that this raises testosterone or improves sperm quality. It is promoted mainly in biohacking communities and has been mentioned in looksmaxxing discussions of hormone optimisation.
claims: Sunlight or red light on the testes raises testosterone.
Red light improves sperm quality.
Red light therapy generally is a proven healing tool.

name: Scrotal cooling / ball icing
summary: Chilling the testes with ice or cold packs to support sperm or testosterone; rooted in real testicular physiology but untested as a practice.
lead: Scrotal cooling, informally 'ball icing', is a fringe practice in which men apply ice, cold packs or cold water to the scrotum, hoping to improve sperm quality or testosterone. It is discussed in biohacking and fertility-optimisation circles and occasionally on looksmaxxing forums.
claims: Cooling the testes improves sperm production.
Cooling raises testosterone.
Heat harms sperm, so cooling is protective.

name: Loose underwear / avoiding heat
summary: Wearing boxers and keeping laptops and heat away from the groin to protect sperm and testosterone; grounded in testicular heat sensitivity, with thin direct evidence in the sources reviewed.
lead: Loose underwear and heat avoidance is a lifestyle practice in which men wear boxers rather than snug briefs and avoid prolonged heat at the groin, such as a laptop on the lap, with the aim of protecting sperm quality and testosterone.
claims: Tight underwear overheats the testes and lowers sperm quality.
Laptops on the lap harm fertility.
Avoiding heat raises testosterone.

name: Phone-in-pocket / EMF avoidance
summary: Keeping phones away from the groin to avoid radiation harming sperm or testosterone; major health bodies find no established harm, though research continues.
lead: Phone-in-pocket or EMF avoidance is a lifestyle practice in which men keep mobile phones out of trouser pockets and sometimes limit exposure to wireless devices in general, out of concern that radiofrequency electromagnetic fields reduce sperm quality or testosterone.
claims: Carrying a phone in the pocket lowers sperm quality.
Phone radiation lowers testosterone.
Wireless radiation, including 5G, is broadly harmful.

name: Cortisol management / stress reduction
summary: Lowering stress and 'cortisol spikes' to protect testosterone, skin and facial leanness; cortisol is real physiology, but 'managing' it for looks is largely untested.
lead: Cortisol management, or stress reduction, is a lifestyle practice in which men try to lower cortisol through sleep, relaxation, diet and avoiding stressors, usually to protect testosterone, reduce facial puffiness and improve skin and body composition. 'Cortisol spike' is also a common forum phrase for momentary stress.
claims: High cortisol makes the face puffy and lowers testosterone, so it should be reduced.
Morning cortisol is good and only night-time elevation matters.
Poor sleep raises cortisol and hurts appearance.
Stressful events cause 'cortisol spikes'.

name: Fluoride avoidance
summary: Skipping fluoride in water and toothpaste for hormone and brain claims; the testosterone angle has no study behind it.
lead: Fluoride avoidance is the practice of limiting or eliminating fluoride exposure, usually by filtering tap water, choosing fluoride-free toothpaste, or avoiding fluoridated products. In looksmaxxing and wider wellness communities it is discussed mainly in connection with claims that fluoride lowers testosterone, calcifies the pineal gland, or harms cognition, and that avoiding it therefore supports hormonal health and appearance .
claims: Fluoride lowers testosterone, so avoiding it supports masculine development.
Fluoride calcifies the pineal gland.
Fluoride exposure lowers IQ.
High fluoride intake causes dental fluorosis.

name: Sperm retention / abstinence rituals
summary: Avoiding ejaculation for energy and looks; the headline testosterone study was retracted and researchers report anxiety risks.
lead: Semen retention is the practice of deliberately avoiding ejaculation, often for weeks or months, and sometimes extended to avoiding masturbation and pornography as in the NoFap movement. In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a way to gain energy, focus, confidence and attractiveness .
claims: Retention increases energy, motivation and workout drive.
Retention raises testosterone.
Retention makes you more attractive to women.
Retention carries anxiety or harm risks.

name: Looksmaxxing "Testosterone maxxing"
summary: The forum push to raise testosterone for muscle, leanness and looks, from sleep and sprints to prescription drugs.
lead: Testosterone maxxing is the looksmaxxing term for trying to raise or optimize testosterone levels, on the belief that higher testosterone improves muscle, leanness, facial masculinity and confidence. Forum guides divide it into lifestyle measures, such as strength training, sprinting, sunlight and sleep, and pharmaceutical routes .
claims: Sprinting, sunlight and sleep raise testosterone.
Higher testosterone makes you more attractive.
Enclomiphene and similar drugs are a route to higher testosterone.
Celebrity tips like eating raw onions and smoking cigars raise testosterone.

name: Sleep on your back (anti-wrinkle)
summary: Sleeping face-up to dodge sleep lines; plausible habit, untested for wrinkles.
lead: Sleeping on the back is promoted in appearance communities as a way to avoid 'sleep lines' and facial compression from pressing the face into a pillow. Proponents say side and stomach sleeping fold the skin night after night .
claims: Side and stomach sleeping cause lasting sleep wrinkles.
Back sleeping prevents facial wrinkles.

name: Apigenin
summary: Chamomile flavone in sleep stacks; GABA-binding in the lab, no sleep or looks trial found.
lead: Apigenin (4',5,7-trihydroxyflavone) is a plant flavone found in parsley, celery, celeriac and especially chamomile, where it makes up about 68 percent of the flavonoids in the flowers . It is sold as a dietary supplement and became popular in sleep-supplement discussion, where it is often paired with magnesium and theanine.
claims: Apigenin before bed improves sleep quality.
Apigenin inhibits CD38 and raises NAD+ for anti-aging.
Apigenin has estrogenic effects.

name: L-theanine
summary: Tea amino acid used as a cheap calming, focus supplement; small studies show stress effects, regulators call evidence insufficient.
lead: L-theanine is a non-proteinogenic amino acid found mainly in tea leaves (Camellia sinensis) and sold as a supplement for relaxation, focus and sleep, often alongside caffeine . It was identified in green tea in 1949 and isolated from gyokuro leaves in 1950 .
claims: L-theanine calms anxiety without sedation.
Combining it with caffeine improves focus.
It helps focus on low sleep.
It can backfire in the morning.

name: Magnesium threonate
summary: A brain-targeted magnesium salt taken at night for sleep; the idea rests on rat data and human proof is thin.
lead: Magnesium L-threonate is a salt of magnesium and threonic acid, a metabolite of vitamin C, sold as an oral dietary supplement under names such as Magtein. It is marketed as a form of magnesium intended to raise magnesium levels in the brain, and in appearance and recovery communities it is taken mainly in the evening for sleep, calm and cognition rather than for any direct effect on facial or bodily features.
claims: Threonate crosses into the brain better than other magnesium forms
It improves sleep quality

name: Huberman sleep stack
summary: A bedtime trio of magnesium threonate, apigenin and theanine popularized by a podcaster; the combination itself is untested.
lead: The Huberman sleep stack is a bedtime supplement combination, commonly described as magnesium threonate, apigenin and theanine, associated with Stanford neuroscientist and podcaster Andrew Huberman. It circulates in sleep and recovery discussions as a way to improve sleep, which some in appearance communities treat as a foundation for skin, energy and looks.

name: Inositol
summary: A sugar-alcohol supplement studied mainly for PCOS; its looksmaxxing sleep and growth claims are untested.
lead: Inositol is a sugar alcohol with the formula C6H12O6 that is a component of cell structures and acts as a signaling molecule in eukaryotic cells; myo-inositol is the most abundant form, and D-chiro-inositol is another isomer sold as a supplement . It is found in fruit (oranges and cantaloupe especially), beans, nuts and grains, and is also made in the body, mainly in the kidneys .
claims: D-chiro-inositol raises testosterone and myo-inositol helps glucose and lipids
Myo-inositol lowers androgens and could stunt mandibular growth

name: Valerian root
summary: A classic herbal sleep aid with mixed trial results and some withdrawal and sedative-interaction cautions.
lead: Valerian is a perennial plant (Valeriana officinalis) native to Europe and southwestern Asia whose dried root is a traditional herbal remedy and a common over-the-counter supplement, mainly for sleep and nervous tension . In looksmaxxing and recovery communities it appears in bedtime and anxiety-calming routines.

name: Passionflower / chamomile tea
summary: A traditional bedtime herbal tea; popular for relaxation, with little trial evidence for sleep.
lead: Passionflower and chamomile tea is an herbal infusion drunk before bed for relaxation and sleep. Chamomile tea is made from the dried flowers of German chamomile or Roman chamomile , and passionflower (Passiflora incarnata, or maypop) is a plant whose dried aerial parts are listed in the European and British Pharmacopoeias .

name: Tart cherry juice
summary: A sour-cherry juice used for recovery and as a melatonin source; trials are small and sleep results unreviewed here.
lead: Tart cherry juice is juice from sour cherries (Prunus cerasus), most commonly the Montmorency cultivar, grown largely in Michigan . It is drunk or taken as concentrate for exercise recovery and sleep, and appears in recovery and sleep routines in appearance communities.

name: Kiwi before bed
summary: Eating kiwifruit in the evening is proposed as a food-based sleep aid; the encyclopedic sources reviewed offer little on it.
lead: Eating kiwifruit before bed is a food-based practice that some people adopt for sleep. Wikipedia's kiwifruit article describes the fruit as about 83% water, rich in vitamin C and vitamin K, and notes allergy risk, but does not discuss sleep effects .

name: GABA supplement
summary: Oral GABA is sold as a calming, sleep-friendly supplement, but whether it reaches the brain is debated and appearance-relevant human data are essentially absent.
lead: Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter of the mammalian central nervous system and is also sold as an oral dietary supplement in many countries .
claims: Taking GABA makes you calm and socially relaxed

name: Phenibut
summary: A Soviet-era GABA-B tranquilizer sold online as a 'nootropic' and used for social ease; tolerance and withdrawal are well documented, human trial data are scarce.
lead: Phenibut (beta-phenyl-gamma-aminobutyric acid) is a central nervous system depressant structurally related to the neurotransmitter GABA. It was developed in the Soviet Union and entered clinical use in Russia in the 1960s as a tranquilizer with cognition-enhancing ('nootropic') properties .
claims: Phenibut is a 'low inhib' drug that makes you confident and sociable
Women respond better to you on phenibut
It can be used frequently without trouble
Combining it with alcohol or kratom enhances the effect

name: Diphenhydramine / doxylamine sleep aids
summary: Over-the-counter sedating antihistamines used for sleep; guideline bodies rate their insomnia evidence poorly and they carry anticholinergic effects.
lead: Diphenhydramine is a first-generation H1 antihistamine that is a common ingredient in nonprescription sleep aids; the related doxylamine is used similarly . It was discovered in 1943 by George Rieveschl and Fred Huber and was the first FDA-approved prescription antihistamine in the US in 1946 .
